generation.hypothesis: Refining interatomic potentials via atomistic and mesoscale simulations can reduce the sintering temperature by accurately capturing the interparticle diffusion and interaction mechanisms, thereby lowering the activation energy required for densification.
generation.material_initial_state: Powder-based ceramic or metallic precursors processed via conventional high-temperature sintering methods.
generation.intervention: Implementation of advanced atomistic/mesoscale simulations using refined interatomic potentials to re-evaluate particle interactions and diffusion barriers prior to sintering.
generation.conditions: Under standard sintering environments (e.g., conventional furnace atmosphere) applied to well-characterized powders.
generation.structural_mediator: Modification of the potential energy landscape at interparticle contacts leading to decreased activation energy for surface and lattice diffusion.
generation.mechanism: Refined potentials provide a more accurate description of atomic interactions, allowing simulations to predict conditions that favor lower energy barriers for particle rearrangement and densification during sintering.
generation.predicted_outcome: The material is expected to achieve comparable densification quality at a lower sintering temperature, with reduced energy consumption and minimal adverse microstructural changes.
generation.baseline: Conventional sintering processes that rely on standard potentials and require high temperatures to overcome higher diffusion activation energy.
generation.boundary: This approach may be less effective if the powder surfaces are contaminated or if the refined potentials do not adequately capture the true interatomic interactions in complex multicomponent systems.
generation.uncertainty: While simulations support a reduction in activation energy, the exact temperature decrease and its consistency across different material systems remain uncertain without experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of powder samples: one processed using conventional potential models and another using refined interatomic potentials as predicted by advanced simulations. Sinter both sets under incrementally reduced temperatures relative to the conventional regime.
measurements: Activation energy computed via Arrhenius plots from diffusion rates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples processed with refined potentials do not achieve comparable densification and microstructural quality at significantly lower sintering temperatures (with statistically lower activation energies) compared to the conventional samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Melting properties are critical for designing novel materials, especially for discovering high-performance, high-melting refractory materials. Experimental measurements of these properties are extremely challenging due to their high melting temperatures. Complementary theoretical predictions are, therefore, indispensable. One of the most accurate approaches for this purpose is the ab initio free-energy approach based on density functional theory (DFT). However, it generally involves expensive thermodynamic integration using ab initio molecular dynamic simulations. The high computational cost makes high-throughput calculations infeasible. Here, we propose a highly efficient DFT-based method aided by a specially designed machine learning potential. As the machine learning potential can closely reproduce the ab initio phase-space distribution, even for multi-component alloys, the costly thermodynamic integration can be fully substituted with more efficient free energy perturbation calculations. The method achieves overall savings of computational resources by 80% compared to current alternatives. We apply the method to the high-entropy alloy TaVCrW and calculate its melting properties

The CALPHAD-based HTCs

The CALPHAD approach [38] – [40] is currently the only method that can be used to obtain multicomponent phase diagrams with enough accuracy for practical applications without the need of the heavy experimental work [41] . This argument has made the CALPHAD method a key building block in the two largest driving forces in materials engineering today—ICME (Integrated computational materials engineering) [42] and MGI (Materials Genome Initiative) [43] . The application of the CALPHAD method requires both the thermodynamic database to provide the Gibbs energies (as a function of pressure, temperature, and composition) for the individual phases and the computational software to calculate the equilibrium state by an energy-minimization procedure. Over the past three decades, the development of consistent multicomponent thermodynamic databases has grown steadily, and several commercial software, such as Pandat TM [44] , Thermo-Calc [45] and FactSage [46] , has become available.
